The Unified Model Graph Three Questions About Every Quantity

The notation rests on a typology of the quantities a statistical model mentions. Any such quantity, a test score, a latent trait, a factor loading, a class membership, a design constant, can be classified by its answers to three questions, and the three answers are logically independent of one another. The existing conventions collapse these questions into fewer symbols than the answers require, and that collapse is where their ambiguities begin.

The UMG assigns each question its own visual channel, so every combination of answers has its own appearance on the page.

The first question concerns observability: is the quantity recorded in the data, or is it inferred from the data through the model? An item response is recorded; the ability assumed to underlie it is inferred. The distinction matters because observed and latent quantities play different roles in estimation and in validity arguments, and because a reader must be able to see which parts of a figure the data constrain directly. The UMG encodes observability with fill: observed quantities are shaded, latent quantities are open.

The second question concerns support: does the quantity take values on a continuum, or in a finite set of categories? A factor score and a reaction time are continuous; a latent class and a binary response are categorical. Support determines the mathematical form of every distribution attached to the quantity, and, for latent variables, it is the difference between a factor model and a mixture model. The UMG encodes support with shape: circles for continuous quantities, squares for categorical ones.

The third question concerns inferential role: how does the quantity enter the likelihood? Four roles cover the models in scope. A random variable carries a probability distribution. A parameter is a fixed unknown that estimation targets. A deterministic quantity is an exact function of other quantities, such as a sum score. A constant is a value fixed by design, such as the unit constant that carries a mean. The UMG encodes role with the outline: a single border for a random variable, an open diamond for a parameter, a double border for a deterministic quantity, and a triangle for a constant, the last inherited from the Reticular Action Model (McArdle & McDonald, 1984).

The independence of the three questions is the point of the typology. Observability does not determine support: a latent variable may be continuous, as a factor is, or categorical, as a class is. Role does not follow from the other two: on a frequentist reading a loading is a fixed unknown, and on a Bayesian reading the same loading is a random variable with a prior. The classic structural equation lexicon offers a single contrast, rectangle versus ellipse, and that one contrast suffices only where observability, support, and role happen to move together, which they do in single-level linear models with continuous variables and nowhere else in the modern repertoire. Separating the three questions is what lets the notation reach that repertoire. It also generates symbols rather than stipulating them: a latent class is latent, categorical, and random, so it is drawn as an open square with a single border, an object no older convention possesses and this notation did not have to invent. Figure 2 displays the complete lexicon, and Table 4 states which visual channel carries which meaning.

The channel assignments follow the graphical perception literature. Value and shape suit nominal distinctions such as observed versus latent (Bertin, 1983), and the magnitude The UMG Lexicon (a) that repeats, labeled by its index.

A measurement model drawn once inside a person plate repeats independently for every person. Nested plates express hierarchy, such as occasions within persons. Overlapping plates express crossing, such as persons by items. The plate states the exchangeability assumption that justifies pooling. The classic path diagram leaves that assumption to the reader.

A small badge in the corner states whether the figure makes a causal claim. Under the statistical badge, the arrows describe only how the joint distribution factors. Under the structural badge, the directed edges among substantive quantities are asserted to be stable under intervention, which makes the figure a causal model in the sense of Pearl (1995).

Figures the Notation Refuses

A notation must also say which figures are not allowed. Some arrangements of the symbols above look like models but describe none, and if such figures were permitted, no

W1 (Acyclicity).

Following the directed edges, stochastic, deterministic, or mixing, must never lead from a vertex back to itself. A directed cycle would leave no order in which the model could generate its quantities, so no factorization of the joint distribution would exist.

W2 (Sources).

Every vertex with no incoming edge must be able to start the generative account. Four kinds of vertex can: a parameter, a constant, an observed random vertex annotated as conditioned on (the familiar fixed-regressor convention), and a random vertex that carries its own unconditional distribution. A bare random vertex with no distribution and no parents gives the model no way to generate it, and the package warns about it.

W3 (Covariance locality).

A covariance edge may join only two random vertices that both carry Gaussian annotations, and it then declares one free covariance between their disturbances. This blocks meaningless associations, such as a covariance between a parameter and a constant, which would assert an association between quantities that do not vary jointly. One further clause keeps the generative order intact: merge every covariance-connected group of vertices into a single vertex, and the directed graph that remains must still be acyclic.

W4 (Mixing).

A mixing edge must start at a latent categorical random vertex and must point at a parameter or a distribution annotation, never at an observed vertex. The rule encodes what a mixture is: class membership switches the regime that generates the data, so it acts on parameters, not on a data point directly. An edge from a continuous latent vertex, or from an observed grouping variable, is not mixing and is refused; an observed grouping variable enters as an ordinary predictor instead.

W5 (Plate coherence).

Plates must fit together, and edges must respect them. Three clauses say how. First, any two plates must be disjoint, nested, or explicitly declared crossed, the nesting must not cycle, and a vertex inside a nested plate belongs to every enclosing plate. Second, a covariance edge may join only vertices with the same plate membership, because a covariance between quantities replicated over different index sets is not defined. Third, a directed edge is licensed only when every plate containing its source also contains its target; otherwise one copy of the target would have to depend on many copies of the source. This is the clause that keeps crossed designs honest: an item parameter, which exists once per item, may point at a response, which exists once per person and item, but not at an ability, which exists once per person. A deterministic aggregate declared as such, a cluster mean for example, is the licensed exception. A mixing edge follows the same logic: every random vertex whose distribution the selected parameter governs must lie inside the plates of the class vertex.

W6 (Annotation totality).

Every part of the figure must carry the information the reading rule needs. Every random vertex carries a distribution, or is an observed source annotated as conditioned on, and every deterministic vertex carries its defining function. Structural equation diagrams may leave the routine annotations implicit; the linear-Gaussian default of that tradition then fills them in, a linear equation in the vertex's parents with a free Gaussian disturbance. This condition makes the reading rule total: it never meets a vertex it cannot read.

Together the six conditions do for the notation what a syntax does for a programming language. They separate the figures that specify a model from the figures that merely resemble one, they localize each failure to a nameable condition, and they make refusal automatic: the package checks all six on construction and reports the violated condition in its error message, as the validation demonstration below shows.

Reading a Diagram as a Model

A well-formed UMG can be read as a likelihood, and the reading is mechanical. Each random vertex contributes a conditional density given its parents. Vertices joined by covariance edges contribute one joint Gaussian block. Plates multiply these contributions over their indices. Mixing edges substitute the parameter copy that the class membership selects. The product of all contributions is the joint distribution of everything the model mentions. Integrating out the continuous latent quantities and summing out the categorical ones gives the likelihood of the observed data. The sum over latent categories is exactly the finite mixture that defines latent class and mixture models (McLachlan & Peel, 2000; Muthén & Shedden, 1999). This construction is the standard one for graphical models (Pearl, 1988; Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen, & Leimer, 1990; Lauritzen, 1996). What is new is the guarantee that it applies to every well-formed figure in this notation.

Two formal results back the guarantee, and both are stated and proved in Part B of the Supplemental Material. The first is soundness and determinacy. For every well-formed UMG, the construction above yields a valid likelihood, the result does not depend on the order in which the figure is read, and the figure corresponds to exactly one family of observed-data distributions. In short, the diagram is not a picture of the model. It is the model, drawn. The second result is coverage. Every model built from parametric conditionals, Gaussian covariance blocks, nested or crossed replication, and finite mixing over categorical latent variables has a well-formed UMG. This class includes confirmatory and exploratory factor models, linear and generalized structural equation models, the standard item response families, generalized linear mixed and latent growth models, latent class, latent profile, and growth mixture models, diagnostic classification models, and the

Bayesian extension of any of them. The examples in this article illustrate the coverage result; they do not substitute for it. Where coverage ends, at continuous-time dynamics, at nonparametric Bayesian structures, and at estimated networks, the boundary is stated in the Discussion. Three further results, also proved in Part B of the Supplemental Material, show that the older conventions are special cases. Restrict the notation to one person plate, continuous variables, linear-Gaussian annotations, and the statistical badge, and it reduces to the recursive path diagram of the Reticular Action Model (McArdle & McDonald, 1984; Bollen, 1989). Restrict it to diagrams without covariance edges in which every parameter has a prior, and it reduces to plate notation (Buntine, 1994; Koller & Friedman, 2009).

Under the structural badge, replace each covariance edge with a latent common cause, and the directed edges among substantive vertices form a causal directed acyclic graph to which the do-calculus applies (Pearl, 2009). The path diagram and the plate diagram turn out to be the same notation specialized in two directions. Each kept the distinctions the other dropped. That is why the two were never reconcilable on their own terms, and why one notation can contain both.

Parameter Promotion: One Object in Four Positions

The most useful single idea in the notation starts from the simplest model psychologists fit. Figure 3, panel (a), is an ordinary regression. The predictor and outcome are shaded circles inside a person plate. The coefficient β, which the path tradition writes as a label on the arrow, is drawn as a diamond outside the plate, feeding the arrow it would have labeled. Nothing about the model has changed. The label has become an object. Now relocate the diamond. Move it inside the plate and give it a distribution across persons, and the fixed coefficient becomes a random effect (panel b). This is the multilevel move that path-diagram syntax cannot draw, done by moving one vertex (Curran & Bauer, 2007; Mehta & Neale, 2005). Give the parameter a prior instead, and it becomes the latent quantity of a Bayesian model; the diamond turns into an open circle whose parents are the constants of the prior (panel c). Point a mixing edge from a latent class vertex at it, and the single coefficient becomes a set of class-specific coefficients; the model is now a mixture (panel d). A fixed effect, a random effect, a Bayesian prior, and a class-specific parameter are one graphical object in four positions.

The statistical content of this observation is not new. Random effects are latent variables, a prior turns a parameter into a random variable, and a mixture switches parameters with a latent class. These are the unifying insights of generalized latent variable modeling (Muthén, 2002; Rabe-Hesketh, Skrondal, & Pickles, 2004; Skrondal & Rabe-Hesketh, 2004) and hierarchical Bayesian practice (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013; Kruschke, 2015). What is new is graphical. The four positions look different on the page, the move between them is one relocation, and the compound figures compose.

The payoff can be computed. The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model of (a) x i y i β i = 1, . . . , N fixed effect: one β, outside the plate (b) random effect: β i inside the person plate,

The umg Package

A notation spreads through software, so the notation comes with software. This section describes the package's concept, design, and functions. Part A of the Supplemental Material complements it with installation instructions and a complete worked example; the two are meant to be read together.

The central design decision is that the diagram itself is the object the software manipulates. The R package umg (Yu, 2026) represents a UMG as a typed data structure that carries everything the notation defines: the vertices with their observability, support, and role; the typed edges; the plates with their nesting and crossing declarations; the distribution annotations; and the badge. Every operation in the package reads or writes this one structure. Because the structure carries the full typing, the well-formedness conditions become mechanical checks, and the package runs them on construction. A directed cycle is refused (W1). A covariance edge that joins non-random vertices is refused (the first clause of W3). A mixing edge with an ill-typed source or target is refused (W4).

An edge or plate declaration that breaks the plate rules is refused (all clauses of W5, including index licensing). A source vertex without a distribution draws a warning (W2), and the linear-Gaussian defaults are supplied where W6 permits them. A figure that does not denote a model is never drawn.

The functions form four groups. Construction functions build the object: the constructors umg_node(), umg_edge(), umg_plate(), and umg_model() assemble a diagram element by element, and one-line builders such as umg_factor(), umg_growth(), umg_mixture(), and umg_riclpm() return ready diagrams for the common families.

Translation functions connect the object to estimation software: umg_from_lavaan(), umg_from_lmer(), and their counterparts for mirt, brms, blavaan, OpenMx, and qgraph build a diagram from a fitted object (Rosseel, 2012; D. Bates, Mächler, Bolker, & Walker, 2015; Chalmers, 2012; Neale et al., 2016; Epskamp et al., 2012), and umg_to_lavaan() emits estimation syntax from a diagram. Interrogation functions read the object: umg_validate() checks well-formedness; umg_identify(), with umg_check_scaling(), umg_count_parameters(), and umg_labelswitching(), runs the identification readings; umg_dsep() and umg_implied_ci() derive testable implications; and umg_eda_scaffold() and umg_caterpillar() generate the model-implied data displays.

Rendering functions draw it: the same object renders through four backends, grid, ggplot2, Graphviz, and TikZ, and umg_save() writes any of them to file. Every figure in this article was produced with the TikZ library that accompanies the package.

What a Determinate Diagram Can Do

Because a well-formed UMG fixes the likelihood, the figure is a formal object, and software can operate on it. This section demonstrates six operations. Every demonstration is an archived script with its output, and the numbers quoted here are the numbers the scripts produce.

Validation

The well-formedness conditions are checked on construction .

A three-vertex directed cycle is refused with the message "W1 violated: directed subgraph (dep/det/mix) contains a cycle." A mixing edge whose source is a continuous latent vertex named eta is refused with "W4 violated: mix edge source 'eta' is not a latent categorical random vertex." A mixing edge aimed directly at an observed vertex y is refused with "W4 violated: mix edge targets observed vertex 'y' directly." A covariance edge joining a latent vertex to a parameter lambda is refused with "W3 violated: cov edge eta <-> lambda joins non-random vertices." An edge that the plate structure cannot carry is also refused: aiming an item-plate parameter a at a person-plate ability theta produces "W5 violated: edge a -> theta is not licensed by the index structure (plates of 'a' are not contained in the plates of 'theta')." The well-formed counterpart of each refused figure, for example a latent class vertex selecting a parameter that feeds the observed vertex, is accepted. In the benchmark, no other package refused the cyclic specification, and every package that accepted it drew it.

Round-Trip Translation

A determinate figure can be translated into estimation syntax and back. For a covariance structure, the round trip is exact. Figure 4 shows the operation on the three-factor model of the Holzinger and Swineford data (Holzinger & Swineford, 1939; Rosseel, 2012). The model is fitted in lavaan. The diagram is built from the fitted object. fit <-cfa("visual =~x1 + x2 + x3 textual =~x4 + x5 + x6 speed =~x7 + x8 + x9", data = HolzingerSwineford1939) m <-umg_from_lavaan(fit) # fitted object -> diagram umg_validate(m) # W1 to W6: TRUE cat(umg_to_lavaan(m)) # diagram -> syntax refit <-cfa(umg_to_lavaan(m), data = HolzingerSwineford1939) ## original refit |difference| ## npar 21.000 21.000 0 ## df 24.000 24.000 0 ## chisq 85.306 85.306 0 ## cfi 0.931 0.931 0 ## rmsea 0.092 0.092 0 ## srmr 0.065 0.065 0 ## max |estimate difference| over 24 matched parameters: 2.2e-16

Note. Output abridged from the archived script demo_roundtrip_V01. R (R 4.3.3, lavaan 0.7-2, umg 0.6.0). The diagram built from the fitted object has 12 vertices (9 observed, 3 latent), 9 stochastic edges with the marker loadings fixed at 1, 3 covariance edges, and one person plate. lavaan syntax is emitted from the diagram, and the emitted syntax is refitted. The two fits are identical: 21 free parameters, 24 degrees of freedom, χ 2 (24) = 85.31, CFI = .931, RMSEA = .092, SRMR = .065 in both, with a maximum absolute difference in parameter estimates of 2.2 × 10 -16 across the 24 matched parameters. The same round trip on a linear latent growth model is also exact. The emitted syntax includes the intercept and mean rows, and refitting it with lavaan's growth function reproduces the original fit: 9 free parameters, 5 degrees of freedom, and a maximum absolute difference in estimates of 2.3 × 10 -15 . Translation from the figure is what a preregistration needs. The benchmark found syntax emission in four of the eight packages, in each case from the package's own model object rather than from a typed diagram.

Identification Checks From the Figure

Because the figure fixes the likelihood, necessary conditions of identification can be read from it before estimation. Three readings are implemented. The scaling check inspects every latent continuous vertex for a unit loading or a fixed variance; a constant parent is reported separately as fixing location, not scale. A one-factor diagram without a scaling mark is reported as unscaled. The same diagram with a marker loading or a unit variance passes. The counting rule compares the free quantities in the figure with the distinct covariance moments of the observed vertices. This is the graphical form of the t-rule (Bollen, 1989). The Holzinger and Swineford diagram returns 45 moments, 21 free parameters, and 24 degrees of freedom, matching the fitted model. A two-indicator factor returns -1 and is flagged as under-identified. The four-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel diagram returns 36 moments, 27 free parameters, and 9 degrees of freedom, the published count (Hamaker et al., 2015). With its mean-structure option, the counting rule on the growth diagram returns 14 moments, 9 free parameters, and 5 degrees of freedom, matching lavaan's growth function. The label-switching check reports, for any diagram with a latent class vertex, that the model is identified only up to permutation of the class labels (Bauer, 2007). On the growth mixture diagram it names the class vertex, and the counting rule declares itself inapplicable with a warning, because covariance moments are not a valid check for a mixture. All three readings are necessary conditions only, and they apply to single-level covariance structures. No graphical reading replaces a formal identification analysis. What each reading does is catch a routine error at the drawing board, where it is cheapest to fix.

Testable Implications

Because a diagram without covariance edges reduces to plate notation, the directed Markov property applies, and the conditional independencies a diagram implies can be read off it by d-separation, with covariance edges treated as latent common causes (Lauritzen et al., 1990). On the mediation diagram of Figure 9 with a direct path, X and Y are reported dependent given M and marginally. With the direct path removed, they are reported independent given M . With the direct path restored and a latent confounder of M and Y added, X and Y remain dependent given M ; X and the confounder are marginally independent; and conditioning on M makes them dependent, because M is a collider on the path between them. The back-door path from M to Y through the confounder cannot be blocked by observed variables, so neither the effect of M on Y nor the direct effect of X adjusted for M is identified while the confounder is unmeasured (Pearl, 1995). Every verdict was cross-checked against dagitty (Textor et al., 2016)

Model-Implied Data Displays

Every motif in a UMG implies a display of the data that would test it. A dependence edge between continuous quantities implies the scatterplot that would expose a nonlinear relation behind a linear coefficient. A latent class vertex implies the marginal density that gives a first check, not a decisive one, on whether the classes are separable or an artifact of skew (Bauer, 2007). A plate implies the trellis of small multiples across its index. A random-coefficient vertex implies the spaghetti plot of person-specific trajectories. A covariance block implies the correlation map among the variables it joins. Figure 5 shows three such displays generated from diagram objects, not from hand-written plotting code.

The left panel shows the trajectories implied by the random-coefficient vertex of the sleepstudy growth diagram (Belenky et al., 2003; D. Bates et al., 2015). The middle panel shows the observed correlation map implied by the covariance block of the Holzinger and Swineford diagram. The right panel shows the marginal density implied by the latent class vertex of a growth mixture diagram on simulated data. Read forward, a diagram is a model to be fitted. Read backward, it is a checklist of the displays that would test it.

Consulting the displays before fitting serves discovery; consulting them after serves Note. Left: person-specific reaction-time trajectories over days of sleep restriction, implied by the random-coefficient vertex of the growth diagram (sleepstudy data; the heavy line is the pooled least-squares line). Middle: observed correlation map among the nine tests, implied by the covariance block of the Holzinger and Swineford diagram. Right: marginal density of an indicator, implied by the latent class vertex of a growth mixture diagram (simulated two-class data). Each panel was produced by one call on its diagram object and the data.

diagnosis (Tukey, 1977). What the notation discourages is the third path, in which a model is quietly revised to match a display and reported as planned (Wagenmakers, Wetzels, Borsboom, van der Maas, & Kievit, 2012).

Versioned Specification

A determinate figure can be differenced. The package exposes a diagram's vertices and edges as data frames, so a preregistered diagram and its estimated successor can be compared with ordinary set operations. For the Holzinger and Swineford model, comparing the preregistered three-factor diagram with a final diagram in which the ninth test also loads on the visual factor returns exactly one added edge, no removed edges, and an identical vertex set. The counting rule reports the change from 24 to 23 degrees of freedom.

Revising a model during analysis is not the problem the replication literature identified.

Reporting the revised model as if it had been planned is (Wagenmakers et al., 2012). A figure that can be versioned and diffed like a script makes the revision visible.

Drawing the Working Models of Psychology

The case for the notation is made by drawing the models psychologists fit. Four illustrations follow. Each uses a feature the path diagram lacks, and each connects to one of the operations above. Every figure was drawn with the TikZ library that accompanies the package. A gallery of fifteen model families, with the code that builds each one, is in the OSF repository.

Measurement: Confirmatory Factor Analysis

The natural starting point is the model the field draws best. Figure 6 shows the three-factor model of nine cognitive tests (Holzinger & Swineford, 1939)

Crossed Designs: Item Response Theory

Item response models break the classic convention immediately. The responses are categorical. The item parameters are neither latent constructs nor observed data; they are fixed unknowns. Persons and items are crossed, not nested, because every person answers every item (Lord & Novick, 1968; Embretson & Reise, 2000).

Hierarchy and Composition: Growth and Growth Mixture Models

The multilevel model is where the path diagram fails most visibly, and where promotion pays off most clearly. Figure 8, panel (a), draws the standard analysis of the sleepstudy data (Belenky et al., 2003; D. Bates et al., 2015). tradition (Mehta & Neale, 2005); the plate form is preferable because it states the pooling assumption the panels leave implicit. Panel (b) is the strongest test of composition: the growth mixture model, which supposes unobserved subgroups of persons, each with its own trajectory (Muthén & Shedden, 1999; Bauer, 2007; Nagin, 2005). The latent class is an open square. Mixing edges state that class membership selects the growth-factor means. The mixing proportions are a parameter vertex feeding the class vertex. Everything else is panel (a). The compound model is the two component diagrams overlaid, not a third template to memorize. The figure also shows a known fragility as a visible path. Every class-specific parameter is reached only through a mixing edge from the class vertex, so a misspecified within-class distribution propagates directly to the estimated number of classes (Bauer, 2007). Remove the growth structure and the same construction is the latent class and latent profile model (Lazarsfeld & Henry, 1968). Remove the mixing edges and it is panel (a) again. The label-switching check demonstrated above attaches to the open square.

Marking the Causal Claim

The last illustration concerns the badge, not a new model. Figure 9 draws the same mediation structure twice. Under the statistical badge, the arrows license only a decomposition of the joint distribution into regressions. That is the reading the data alone support. Under the structural badge, the same topology gains a latent confounder of the mediator and the outcome, and the causal reading becomes available and disciplined. The d-separation reading demonstrated above, applied to the structural panel, shows that the back-door path from the mediator to the outcome cannot be blocked by observed variables, and that conditioning on the mediator opens a collider path from the exposure to the confounder. Neither the mediator's effect nor the direct effect adjusted for the mediator is identified unless the confounder is measured (Pearl, 1995; Rohrer, 2018).

Coverage Beyond the Illustrations

The four illustrations are representatives, not special cases the notation was tuned to fit. Figure 10 gathers four further families drawn from the same symbols with no new vocabulary. The bifactor model adds a general factor loading on every indicator (Reise, 2012). The MIMIC model lets an observed covariate predict a latent factor and, through a direct path to one indicator, expresses differential item functioning, the measurement non-invariance that comparative research must detect before group comparisons are meaningful (Jöreskog & Goldberger, 1975; Meredith, 1993). The psychometric network

Discussion

The argument of this article is short. A model diagram should let the reader recover the model that was fitted. The conventions psychology uses do not, for the models psychologists now fit most. A notation that types quantities on three dimensions, types dependencies, marks replication, and states its license does, and the guarantee is proved Three limits bound the claims. The first is scope. The coverage result includes the directed, finitely mixed, parametric models that dominate current practice. It stops short of continuous-time and dynamic structural equation models, of nonparametric Bayesian structures whose dimension is itself unknown, and of estimated networks, which the notation can display but not fully specify because they are pictures of fitted quantities (Borsboom & Cramer, 2013). Extending the plate machinery to random and growing index sets is the next formal problem.

The second limit is the implementation. Version 0.6.0 of umg is the version executed for every result here, and it has three known gaps. It stores distribution annotations but does not print them through its automatic renderers, and it leaves residual variances implicit in rendered figures. Its counting and scaling readings apply to single-level covariance structures. In the MIMIC and formative motifs, it treats the observed causes as modeled rather than conditioned on, so their free covariances are omitted from the count.

Each gap is recorded in the archived materials with reproduction code. None of the formal results depends on the implementation.

The third limit concerns readers, and it is the one the notation now makes testable.

The channel allocation follows the graphical perception literature (Cleveland & McGill, 1984), but no experiment here shows that UMG figures are read faster or misread less often than conventional figures. The natural study is a preregistered within-subjects comparison.

Graduate students and reviewers see figures in conventional notation and in the UMG.

They identify which quantities are latent, which effects vary across persons, how many latent classes the model posits, whether a causal reading is licensed, and how many free parameters the model has. Accuracy and response time are scored and analyzed with crossed random effects for participants and items. The exhibits of Figure 1 supply the stimuli on which the notations should differ most, and the materials of this article supply the figures. Until that study is run, the perceptual and pedagogical benefits of the notation are hypotheses with a design attached.

Two consequences for practice do not wait on that study. First, determinacy can be demanded of a figure in any notation. Typed quantities, typed dependencies, explicit replication, and a declared license can be achieved in a classic path diagram through disciplined use of its own devices plus a caption that states the rest. Reporting standards already ask for completeness in model reporting (Appelbaum et al., 2018; McDonald & Ho, 2002); determinacy gives the figure-level version of that demand, and an audit of how often published figures meet it is the natural companion study. Second, adoption runs through software defaults and teaching. The package renders through the backends researchers already use, and the free channels of Table 4 leave room for the estimate-weighted and color-coded figures applied work needs. For teaching, the promotion figure gives an instructor one thread to follow, from the first regression a student draws to the mixture model the student may one day fit. Whether following that thread improves learning is a hypothesis of the same kind as the comprehension claim, and it should be tested the same way.

remotes::install_github("hsiutingyu/umg", subdir = "umg", ref = "v0.6.0") # Version 0.6.0, from the source tarball in the OSF repository: install.packages("umg_0.6.0.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")

The package imports only base R packages (grid, grDevices, stats, tools, utils). The converters and the ggplot2 backend use suggested packages (lavaan, lme4, mirt, brms, blavaan, OpenMx, qgraph, ggplot2) only when called.

Building a Diagram by Hand

A diagram is built from three constructors: umg_node() for vertices, umg_edge() for edges, and umg_plate() for plates. umg_model() assembles them and validates on construction. The example below is the two-indicator factor diagram from the archived validation script. library(umg) m <-umg_model( nodes = list( umg_node("eta", "$\\eta_i$", observed = FALSE, dist = "N(0, psi)"), umg_node("y1", "$y_{1i}$", observed = TRUE), umg_node("y2", "$y_{2i}$", observed = TRUE) ), edges = list( umg_edge("eta", "y1", "dep", fixed = 1), umg_edge("eta", "y2", "dep", label = "$\\lambda_2$") ), plates = list(umg_plate("person", c("eta", "y1", "y2"), "i = 1, ..., N")) ) umg_validate(m) # TRUE

A figure that breaks a well-formedness condition is refused with a message that names the condition. For example, adding the edges A -> B -> C -> A produces W1 violated: directed subgraph (dep/det/mix) contains a cycle, and aiming an item-plate parameter at a person-plate ability produces W5 violated: edge a -> theta is not licensed by the index structure.

One-Line Builders

Builders return ready diagrams for the common families. Each returns an ordinary umg object that can be edited, checked, and rendered.

umg_factor("F", paste0("y", 1:4)) # one-factor model umg_growth(4) # linear growth, 4 occasions umg_mixture(umg_growth(4), c("I", "S")) # growth mixture model umg_riclpm(waves = 4) # random-intercept CLPM Similar builders cover structural equation, bifactor, formative, item response, mediation, latent class, and network models; the gallery in Supplemental Material S2 builds fifteen families with full code.

Translation To and From Estimation Syntax

umg_from_lavaan() builds a diagram from a fitted lavaan object, umg_from_lmer() from an lme4 formula and data, and umg_to_lavaan() emits lavaan syntax from a diagram. The round trip below is the one reported in the manuscript; the refit is identical to the original (maximum absolute difference in estimates 2.2 × 10 -16 ). -------------------------Latent scaling: 3 latent continuous vertex(es); all scaled Counting rule: 45 data moments, 21 free parameters, df = 24 Implied conditional independencies (observed): 0 Note: necessary conditions only; not a formal identification proof.

The pieces are available separately as umg_check_scaling(), umg_count_parameters() (with a mean-structure option), and umg_labelswitching(). On a mixture diagram, the counting rule declares itself inapplicable with a warning, and the label-switching check names the class vertex.

Testable Implications umg_dsep() answers a single d-separation query, and umg_implied_ci() lists the implied conditional independencies, among observed vertices by default.

umg_dsep(m_med, "X", "Y", given = "M") umg_implied_ci(m_med, observed_only = TRUE) Model-Implied Displays umg_eda_scaffold() returns one ggplot2 display per motif of the diagram, built from the diagram object and a data frame. umg_caterpillar() plots conditional modes of random effects.

sc <-umg_eda_scaffold(m_sleep, data = lme4::sleepstudy, id = "Subject", time = "Days") names(sc) # one display per motif

Rendering and Export plot() draws a diagram with the grid backend. umg_ggplot() (or autoplot()) draws it with ggplot2. umg_to_dot() and umg_render_dot() use Graphviz. umg_to_tikz() emits TikZ code for the style library used in the manuscript, and umg_save() writes any backend to file. umg_layout() and umg_theme() control positions and the free visual channels. plot(m) umg_save(m, "hs_cfa.pdf") cat(umg_to_tikz(m), file = "hs_cfa.tex")

Differencing Two Diagrams

A diagram exposes its vertices and edges as data frames, so a preregistered diagram and its final version can be compared with ordinary set operations. This is the comparison reported in the manuscript. The archived scripts behind these examples are demo_validate, demo_roundtrip, demo_identify, demo_dsep, demo_eda, demo_backends, demo_diff, and demo_gallery, each with its complete output.

Part B: Formal Definitions and Results

This part states the formal results the article relies on and proves them. The machinery is that of directed graphical models (Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen, & Leimer, 1990; Lauritzen, 1996). The reading equations come first, then the definitions, then the results with their proofs.

The Reading Equations

types each vertex by observability O = {obs, lat}, support S = {cont, cat}, and role R = {rv, par, det, const}; Π is a finite set of plates, each a pair (S p , I p ) of a scope S p ⊆ V and a finite index set I p ; and α assigns a conditional density (with respect to a fixed σ-finite measure on the vertex's support) to each vertex of role rv, given its parents, and a measurable function of its parents to each vertex of role det. A vertex of role par that is the target of a mix edge from a categorical vertex c with K values denotes a K-vector θ (1) , . . . , θ (K) ; wherever that parameter enters a density, the value θ (c) is substituted, so that c is a parent of every random vertex whose density involves the parameter. A parameter targeted by mix edges from several categorical vertices denotes an array indexed by the product of their value sets, and a mix edge into a distribution annotation is read the same way, with the annotation's parameters treated as an implicit parameter vertex. For v ∈ V write plates(v) = {p ∈ Π : v ∈ S p } and pa(v) for the set of tails of dep and det edges into v together with the sources of mix edges whose targets enter the density of v. The badge is a flag in {statistical, structural}.

Definition 2 (Well-formedness). G is well-formed when W1 to W6 of the main text hold, with W3 including the condition that the graph obtained by merging each set of covariance-linked vertices into one vertex is acyclic, with W6 exempting observed sources annotated as conditioned on, and with W5 read as: (W5a) for any two plates, S p ∩ S q = ∅, or S p ⊆ S q , or S q ⊆ S p , or the pair is declared crossed, and the inclusion relation is acyclic; (W5b) a vertex in a plate nested in q is in S q ; (W5c) for every edge (u, v, k) with k = dep, plates(u) ⊆ plates(v); for k = det the same holds unless v is annotated as an aggregate over plates(u) \ plates(v); for k = cov, plates(u) = plates(v); and for k = mix with source c, plates(c) ⊆ plates(w) for every random vertex w whose density involves the target.

Definition 3 (Instantiation). The instantiation of G is the graph G * whose vertices are the pairs (v, ι) with v ∈ V and ι a tuple of indices, one from I p for each p ∈ plates(v), and whose edges join (u, ι u ) to (v, ι v ) whenever u ∈ pa(v) and ι u is the restriction of ι v to plates(u); for a deterministic aggregate v, the parents of (v, ι v ) are all (u, ι u ) whose restriction to plates(v) equals ι v . A mix-targeted parameter vertex is instantiated over its own plates as usual; the copy (c, ι c ) of its source selects which of its K values enters each density that involves it.

W5c is exactly the condition under which the restrictions in Definition 3 are defined, so every instantiated vertex has a well-defined set of instantiated parents, each appearing once.

Definition 4 (Induced family). Let θ collect the values of the par vertices, the free edge labels, and the free quantities of the annotations (variances, covariances, link and mixing parameters), let Θ be the set of values for which every annotation is a density (positive definite covariance blocks, mixing proportions on the simplex), and fix the const vertices. Observed source vertices annotated as conditioned on are held fixed throughout. Equation 1 applied to G * defines p(V * rv ; θ); Equation 2 defines L(θ) as the marginal density of the observed instantiated vertices given the conditioned sources. The induced family is {L(• ; θ) : θ ∈ Θ}.

Soundness and Determinacy

Result 1 (Soundness and determinacy). Let G be a well-formed UMG. Then the righthand side of Equation 1 is a probability density for every value of the free quantities in the admissible parameter set, it does not depend on the order in which vertices, blocks, or plates are enumerated, and Equation 2 is well defined. Consequently G determines exactly one family of observed-data distributions, indexed by its parameter vertices, free edge labels, and free annotation quantities.

Proof. Let G be well-formed, G * its instantiation, and θ ∈ Θ. (i) The instantiated directed graph is acyclic: a directed cycle in G * projects onto a directed closed walk in G, which W1 forbids. Let the instantiated random vertices be partitioned into blocks, each block a maximal set joined by cov edges; by W5c every cov edge joins vertices with identical plate membership, so blocks are well defined after instantiation. The quotient graph over blocks is acyclic, because it is the instantiation of the merged graph that the second clause of W3 requires to be acyclic, and a cycle within one block is excluded by W1. Choose a topological order of the blocks. By W6 every random vertex carries a conditional density given its parents, and by W3 every block with more than one vertex is jointly Gaussian given its external parents, its internal directed edges absorbed into the block's reduced form, with a disturbance covariance matrix whose free off-diagonal elements are those marked by cov edges; for θ ∈ Θ that covariance is positive definite, so the block density is a valid conditional density. By W2 every block without parents carries an unconditional density or is held fixed. The product of conditional densities along a topological order is a joint density, since integrating the last factor over its own variables gives one and the argument repeats down the order (Lauritzen et al., 1990). (ii) The product over a finite index set is commutative, so the value does not depend on the topological order chosen or on the order in which plates are enumerated; and instantiation commutes with factorization because, by Definition 3, the parents of an instantiated vertex are determined by the edges of G and the index tuple alone. (iii) Marginalizing a joint density over a subset of its variables, by integration over continuous latent vertices and summation over categorical ones, yields a density of the remaining variables for every θ, so L(θ) is well defined. Finally, each step above is a function of (V, E, τ, Π, α) and θ; hence the map from well-formed diagrams to induced families is a function, and G determines exactly one family.

Result 1 concerns the map from the tuple (V, E, τ, Π, α) to the family. The map from a drawn figure to the tuple is also a function, because each reserved visual channel of the lexicon (the channel table of the main article) encodes exactly one component of the typing and the W6 defaults are fixed; the composite map from figure to family is therefore a function, which is the sense in which the drawn figure is determinate.

Coverage

Result 2 (Coverage). Let M be the smallest class of models that contains every parametric conditional distribution whose parameters are smooth functions of a linear predictor in its parents, and that is closed under directed composition, jointly Gaussian blocks with structured covariance, independent and identically distributed replication over nested or crossed index sets conditional on the quantities not replicated, and finite mixing over a categorical latent variable. Every model in M admits a well-formed UMG whose induced family under Equations 1 and 2 is the model.

Proof. Define M inductively. Base: a single random variable y with conditional density f (y | η) in a parametric family, where η = g(β ⊤ z) for parents z (possibly empty), a smooth link g, and parameters β. Closure rules: (composition) the joint of two members over disjoint response sets whose union of parent relations is acyclic and whose index structures are compatible, in that a quantity shared by both carries the same plate membership in each; (Gaussian block) a set of responses jointly Gaussian given their external parents with covariance free on a specified set of off-diagonal positions; (replication) independent and identically distributed copies of a member over a finite index set, conditional on the quantities not replicated, with the index set nested in or crossed with existing index sets; (mixing) a member whose parameter subvector θ S is replaced by θ (c) S for a categorical latent c with P (c = k) = π k , where c is replicated over the index sets of the responses that depend on θ S or over a subset of them.

For the base, construct G with an rv vertex y annotated f (• | η), vertices for the parents z with dep edges into y, and par vertices (or edge labels) for β; W1, W2, and W6 hold, W3 to W5 are vacuous, and Equation 1 returns f (y | η). Assume the claim for the components of each closure rule and construct: (composition) the union of the two diagrams on shared vertices, acyclic by hypothesis, so W1 holds, with W5 preserved because shared quantities carry the same plate membership in both components, and the product of the two factorizations is the joint; (Gaussian block) add cov edges between the responses in the specified positions, so W3 holds and the block density is the Gaussian with the marked free covariances; (replication) enclose the replicated substructure in a plate (S, I) whose nesting or crossing mirrors the index structure; every edge from an unreplicated quantity into the plate satisfies W5c because the plates of the tail are a subset of the plates of the head, and Equation 1 multiplies the component density over the copies; (mixing) add a lat, cat, rv vertex c inside the plates over which it is replicated, annotated with the categorical distribution π, a par vertex for π feeding c, and mix edges from c to the par vertices in S (or to the annotations that carry θ S ), so W4 holds and W5c holds because every response depending on θ S lies in the plates of c; the sum over the copies of c in Equation 2returns, for each copy ι of the replicated unit, k π k L ι,k (θ), and for an unreplicated c the whole-sample mixture k π k L k (θ). Each construction preserves W1 to W6 and the identity between the induced family and the model, so by induction on the number of rule applications every member of M admits a well-formed UMG whose induced family is the model.

The Three Reductions

Result 3 (Path/RAM reduction). Restrict to UMGs with one person plate, continuous random vertices, linear-Gaussian annotations, the statistical badge, and parameters drawn only as edge labels. Forgetting the fill and role typing and drawing observed vertices as rectangles and latent vertices as ellipses is a bijection onto recursive Reticular Action Model path diagrams for covariance structures whose covariance-linked sets satisfy W3: the directed edges collect into the asymmetric matrix, the covariance edges and variances into the symmetric matrix, and the fill rule into the filter that selects observed variables (McArdle & McDonald, 1984; Bollen, 1989).

Result 4 (Plate/PGM reduction). Restrict to UMGs without covariance edges in which every parameter has been given a prior. Forgetting the role dimension leaves fill and shape, which is the plate notation of Bayesian graphical modeling (Buntine, 1994; Koller & Friedman, 2009; Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013), to which the directed Markov property and d-separation apply (Lauritzen et al., 1990).

Result 5 (Causal reduction). Under the structural badge, the subgraph of stochastic edges among substantive vertices, after each covariance edge is replaced by a latent common cause, is a causal directed acyclic graph in the sense of Pearl (2009), and the do-calculus applies to it. Under the statistical badge no interventional claim is licensed, whatever the direction of the edges.

Proof of Result 3. Under the restriction, every vertex is continuous and random, the directed graph is acyclic by W1 so the model is recursive, the single plate contributes a product over persons of identical factors, and every annotation is linear-Gaussian with parameters on the edges; the mean structure, which the Reticular Action Model carries with a unit constant, extends the argument with a const vertex and is omitted here. Write A for the matrix whose (i, j) entry is the label of the dep edge from j to i (zero if absent), S for the symmetric matrix whose off-diagonal entries are the labels of cov edges and whose diagonal entries are the variance annotations, and F for the selection matrix of observed vertices, read from fill. Equation 1 then states that the vector of all vertices ν satisfies ν = Aν + ζ with Cov(ζ) = S, so the observed covariance is F (I -A) -1 S(I -A) -⊤ F ⊤ , which is the Reticular Action Model (McArdle & McDonald, 1984). Conversely any recursive RAM triple (A, S, F ) whose covariancelinked sets satisfy the merged-graph clause of W3 defines the edges, variances, and fills of a restricted UMG. The two maps are inverse on this class, hence a bijection.

Proof of Result 4. Without cov edges every block is a single vertex, and with every parameter given a prior every non-constant vertex has role rv or det; a parameter that carries a prior and is targeted by a mix edge becomes K random vertices in a plate over k, on which each child depends together with c, and a deterministic vertex is a degenerate conditional. Forgetting role leaves fill (observed versus latent) and shape (continuous circles, categorical squares), which is the plate notation of Bayesian graphical modeling; the instantiated graph is a directed acyclic graph over random variables in which each vertex carries a conditional density given its parents, a Bayesian network with plates (Buntine, 1994; Koller & Friedman, 2009), and the directed Markov property and hence d-separation follow from the factorization (Lauritzen et al., 1990).

Proof of Result 5. Replace each cov edge between u and v by a new lat vertex with dep edges into u and v; the induced family is unchanged on the interior of the parameter space because a free covariance between two Gaussian disturbances is the marginal of a common latent cause with free loadings (Bollen & Pearl, 2013). The resulting directed graph among substantive vertices is acyclic by W1. Under the structural badge the dep edges are asserted invariant to intervention on their tails, which is the definition of a causal model over that graph (Pearl, 2009), and the do-calculus is a property of such models. Under the statistical badge the same graph is asserted only as a factorization, which licenses d-separation but no interventional claim.

The badge has no counterpart in the older conventions, and its absence is the source of the confusion in panel (c) of Figure 1.

Open Practices Statement

No new data were collected, and no hypotheses were tested; the work was not preregistered. All materials are openly archived on the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/d4xrm. The archive contains the R package umg (version 0.6.0, the version executed for every result reported), the TikZ style library, and the demonstration scripts with their complete output. It also contains the benchmark protocol with every script, rendering, and coded cell; the model gallery with code for fifteen families; the package vignettes; and the Supplemental Material that accompanies this article, a two-part document with the umg package guide (Part A) and the formal definitions and proofs (Part B). The illustrative analyses use openly available data sets: the Holzinger and Swineford data as distributed with lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) and the sleepstudy data as distributed with lme4 (D. Bates et al., 2015); the growth mixture demonstration uses simulated data generated by an archived, seeded script.

Supplemental Material for "The Unified Model

Graph: Drawing the Statistical Models of Psychology"

Hsiu-Ting Yu

Department of Psychology, National Chengchi University, Taipei, Taiwan This document accompanies the article named in the title and has two parts. Part A is a practical guide to the R package umg: installation, building and checking diagrams, translation, identification readings, testable implications, model-implied displays, rendering, and diagram differencing. Every code example comes from the archived demonstration scripts in the OSF repository (https://osf.io/d4xrm), and the printed outputs are the outputs those scripts produce under version 0.6.0. Part B states the formal layer of the article in full: the definition of the Unified Model Graph (UMG) as a mathematical object, the well-formedness conditions W1 to W6 in their precise form, the instantiation and induced family through which a diagram is read as a likelihood, and the proofs of Results 1 to 5. Part B is self-contained: the factorization and likelihood equations of the article are restated there as Equations ( 1) and (2).

Part A: Using the umg Package

The main article describes the package's concept, design, and function groups. This part shows how to install the package and how to use each function group, with worked examples. Every example is executed, with full output, in the archived demonstration scripts in the OSF repository.

Installation

The current release, version 0.6.1, is on CRAN. It differs from version 0.6.0, the version executed for every result in the article, only in documentation and package metadata. The first command below installs the current release; the other two install version 0.6.0.

# Current release, from CRAN: install.packages("umg") # Version 0.6.0, from GitHub: what each convention can express.

figure could be trusted. The UMG therefore comes with six well-formedness conditions, W1 to W6. A figure that satisfies all six specifies exactly one model; a figure that violates any one of them is refused. Each condition can be checked in a single pass over the figure, so software can run all six before drawing anything. The list below states each condition in a working form, together with the modeling error it blocks; Part B of the Supplemental Material states each condition with full formal precision.

Hamaker, Kuiper, and Grasman (2015) fixes the classic cross-lagged panel model by promoting person-level intercepts into the person plate, which separates within-person dynamics from stable between-person differences. In this notation, that revision is the cross-lagged figure with two vertices relocated. The counting rule demonstrated below, applied to the four-wave figure, returns 9 degrees of freedom, the published count. The 27 free parameters it reports are the covariance-structure count, which lavaan's model parser reproduces for the same syntax. Whether a student who has seen one promotion recognizes the other three more easily is a hypothesis about learners. The Discussion states it as such.

Figure 3Parameter Promotion: One Coefficient in Four Positions

Note. (a) Fixed effect: one β outside the plate. (b) Random effect: β i promoted into the person plate with a distribution across persons. (c) Bayesian prior: β promoted to a random vertex whose parents are the constants of the prior. (d) Class-specific: a latent class vertex selects among β (1) , . . . , β (K) through a mixing edge. Shaded circles = observed continuous variables; open circles = latent continuous variables; open square = latent class; diamond = estimated parameter; triangle = known constant.

Two further design choices serve reproducible practice. First, the package core imports only base R packages; lavaan, lme4, and the other modeling packages are suggested dependencies, loaded only when a converter is called, so the diagram machinery itself carries no modeling dependencies. Second, a diagram is generated from a plain-text specification, so it belongs in a replication package the same way analysis code does: the specification can be versioned, diffed against a preregistered predecessor, and recompiled by a reader. Version 0.6.0 is the version executed for every result in this article. It is available on GitHub (https://github.com/hsiutingyu/umg) and as an archived source tarball in the OSF repository. The current release, version 0.6.1, is on CRAN (https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=umg); it changes only documentation and package metadata, so every result reported here is unchanged. Its remaining gaps are stated here rather than discovered later. The automatic renderers do not print stored distribution annotations, and they leave residual variances implicit in rendered figures. The counting and scaling readings apply to single-level covariance structures. In the MIMIC and formative motifs, the observed causes are treated as modeled rather than conditioned on, so their free covariances are omitted from the count. Each gap is recorded in the archived materials with reproduction code. None of the formal results depends on the implementation.

Figure 4

Figure 4Round-Trip Translation Between a Fitted Model and Its Diagram on the corresponding causal graph.

The two agree on every query. The difference is what sits around the graph. The causal-graph packages represent vertices and arrows only. The UMG carries the same graph inside a figure that also types the confounder, draws the parameters as objects, encloses the structure in a plate, and states the license through the badge.

Figure 5

Figure 5Three Exploratory Displays Generated From Diagrams in the classic convention and as a UMG.

The translation is mechanical. The observed tests, bare rectangles in the classic figure, become shaded circles: observed and continuous. The factors remain open circles. The loadings become labeled arrows, with one unit loading per factor fixing the scale. The unique variances become residual stubs. The person plate states the replication over the 301 respondents that the classic figure leaves implicit. The gain at this stage is modest but real. The figure now states, rather than assumes, that the constructs are inferred, that the model repeats across persons, and that the loadings are estimated. Its identification is also on display: each latent vertex carries a scaling mark, and the 21 free quantities against 45 available moments can be recovered by inspection.

Figure 7, panel (a), draws a two-parameter logistic model. The responses are shaded squares at the intersection of two overlapping plates, one for persons and one for items. Ability is an open circle in the

Figure 6Holzinger and Swineford Three-Factor Model: Classic Convention and UMG figure therefore shows the exact sense in which marginal maximum likelihood and hierarchical Bayesian estimation treat one measurement structure under different commitments about the item parameters(Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013;Kruschke, 2015).

The licensing clause of W5 keeps the crossed figure honest. An item parameter may point at a response, which exists once per person and item. It may not point at an ability, which exists once per person.

Each participant has a personal intercept and slope on days of sleep restriction. The two random coefficients are open circles inside the person plate. Their population means are diamonds outside all plates. The covariance edge between them carries the intercept-slope association. The occasion plate nests inside the person plate. The figure shows the distinctions that path-diagram improvisations blur: a fixed effect is a diamond outside the plate, a random effect is a circle inside it, and the difference is one relocation. Hue, size, and stroke weight carry no model meaning. An author can use them for emphasis or for estimated magnitudes, as network figures do, and the model shown by the figure does not change. Whether this allocation makes UMG figures easier to read than conventional figures is a hypothesis about readers, not a demonstrated fact; the Discussion describes the study that would test it.
